transcript.content: Hello. I'm glad you're here today. What brings you in to see me?

I'm here because I know a few people in my department have quietly agreed to block my grants and promotions, and I can’t shake that belief no matter how much my wife or colleagues argue with me. It is incredibly frustrating to feel like I'm the only one who sees what is actually going on.
How long have you been experiencing these concerns about your colleagues blocking your career progress?

This has been going on for about a year now. It really started after I lost out on a major research grant for the second time, and then a younger colleague ended up getting the faculty position I was hoping for.
Have you ever heard voices, seen things, or had other sensory experiences that other people around you couldn't perceive?
No, I have never heard any voices or seen things that others couldn't perceive. My senses are completely normal, and I don't experience anything unusual like that.
Have you had any difficulty organizing your thoughts, or has anyone mentioned that your speech has become hard to follow or confusing?
No, I haven't had any trouble organizing my thoughts, and my mind feels very clear. No one has ever mentioned that my speech is confusing or hard to follow, either.
Apart from this issue at work, have you noticed a significant drop in your motivation, energy, or interest in socializing and doing things you used to enjoy?

My overall energy and motivation are fine, and I still keep up with my teaching assistant duties, grading, and chores at home. I've only been socializing less and skipping department events because I am preoccupied with investigating the committee and avoiding the colleagues I don't trust, not because I've lost interest in things.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a systematized, non-bizarre persecutory delusion (that department colleagues are conspiring to block his grants and promotions) lasting for approximately one year. He does not exhibit hallucinations, disorganized speech, or prominent negative symptoms, and his functioning remains relatively intact outside of the direct impact of his delusion. This clinical picture is highly characteristic of Delusional Disorder (F22.0).
